newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan, euro doubts push dollar to 6-year peak vs mark.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan, euro doubts push dollar to 6-year peak vs mark.

text.p: The dollar surged to its highest level against the German mark in six years on Tuesday, buoyed by soothing remarks from Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan and a growing perception that Europe's planned single currency will be broad-based and weak.

In the first leg of his semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony, Greenspan told a House Banking subcommittee that U.S. growth appeared to be slowing and that he was confident of modest inflation through the end of 1997.
His remarks sent stock and bond prices sharply higher and boosted an already soaring dollar above the 1.82 mark threshold for the first time since August 1991.

"The risk was that Greenspan would come back and say there was a chance of increasing inflation," said Lizbeth Goldberg, assistant vice president of foreign exchange at Bayerische Hypotheken und Wechselbank.
"He did not say that, the bond and stock market took off, and the dollar just followed."

The Dow Jones industrial average soared 154.93 points to close at a record 8,061.65 on Tuesday, while the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond rose 1-22/32. The long bond yield sank to 6.41 percent -- its lowest level in over seven months -- from 6.54 percent at Monday's close.
The dollar ended at 1.8245 marks, the highest level of the day, vs. 1.7965 marks at Monday's close. The dollar fell to 115.00 Japanese yen from 116.15 yen.
Greenspan's remarks added additional fuel to a dollar rally against the mark which began overseas because of mounting doubts about the strength of Europe's planned common currency, known as the euro.

These doubts were sparked on Monday when a French budget audit showed that the country would fail to bring its budget deficit to within 3.0 percent of gross domestic product -- a required level for countries participating in the launch of the euro.

On Tuesday, German officials appeared to welcome French plans to hike taxes on big business and cut spending in order to get closer to the 3.0 percent target, while shrugging off the importance of meeting that precise level.
Without German insistence on a strict interpretation of the criteria for monetary union, many fear that a large number of undisciplined countries will qualify, leading to a weak euro.
These fears were exacerbated when Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Koebnick told German radio on Tuesday that the euro could be stable even if Germany and France missed the targets.

"I think it's clear in the wake of this French audit and tax proposal that the euro is going to go ahead on time and we'll have a soft beginning," said David Gilmore, partner at Foreign Exchange Analytics.
"We have numerous Bundesbank officials saying France is doing all it can to meet the criteria and that that is enough."
In addition to its slide against the dollar, the slumping mark also dropped to its lowest level against the British pound in almost seven years, and fell to 10-month lows against the Swiss franc.

Since neither Britain nor Switzerland are expected to participate in the single currency's launch in 1999, their currencies, along with the dollar, tend to attract "safe-haven" buying when doubts about European monetary union emerge.
Dealers attributed the dollar's poor performance against the yen to the Japanese currency's strength against the mark and to continuing flight from ailing exotic Asian currencies to the yen.
Besieged Southeast Asian currencies stabilised somewhat on Tuesday after weeks of speculative selling, but traders said further damage could be forthcoming.

"This wave of contagion hitting the regional currencies will be a relatively long running affair," said Desmond Supple, head of Asian currency research at BZW Asia. "The danger is that this is a temporary calm we're seeing."
In other trade on Tuesday, the dollar pushed up to 1.4825 Swiss francs from 1.4760 on Monday, and edged up to Canadian $1.3782 from C$1.3775. The British pound rose to $1.6805 from $1.6787 on Monday.
